blocks.text: A Japanese original. Two American parents.
Fuji started with a cross in Fujisaki, Aomori, Japan, in 1939: Ralls Janet (Kokko) × Delicious.

Officially named and registered in 1962, it took its name from its hometown. Today, “Fuji” describes the apple variety; it doesn’t mean the apple in your hand was grown in Japan. Read the origin story ↗
Dense, crisp flesh with plenty of juice. Made for eating fresh.
A sweetness-led profile with gentle acidity, rather than a sharp, tart bite.
A red-to-pink blush over a yellow-green base; color varies by strain and growing conditions.
From its birthplace to orchards across both hemispheres. These are selected growing and export regions, not an exhaustive farm directory.
Fujisaki is where the variety began. Aomori’s apple-growing history and Fuji’s breeding story are closely connected.
Washington’s Wenatchee Valley growers list Fuji among their varieties. New York also grows Fuji, with its own regional growers and seasonal supply.
USDA’s 2024 China fruit report identifies Fuji as the country’s most plentiful apple variety. Production includes fruit for domestic consumption and trade.
Both export Fuji apples. Their opposite growing season helps extend international supply beyond the Northern Hemisphere harvest.

Harvest is seasonal. Shopping can be year-round. Northern and Southern Hemisphere crops, together with refrigerated storage, extend availability. Exact harvest dates and store origins vary by region, season, and supplier.
A typical commercial journey, based on Washington’s packing process. Individual growers, exporters, and retailers may handle fruit differently.
Apples are picked in the orchard and collected into bins before moving to a packing house.
Fruit is washed and inspected. Size, color, shape, internal condition, and maturity help determine its next stop.
Refrigeration slows ripening. Controlled-atmosphere rooms also manage gases to preserve quality for later sale.
Apples are packed for distribution to retailers and other buyers. Imported fruit adds an exporter and importer to the journey.
Inside the process: Washington Apple Commission ↗
Where did your Fuji come from?
Start with the country-of-origin sign or packaging. Then look for a grower or packer name and a lot code. If you want the actual orchard, ask the produce department or the named supplier.
The variety name alone cannot identify a farm, harvest date, or shipping route. A retailer may change suppliers throughout the year.
Start with these US retailers or buy through a regional grower. Listings are examples, not live local inventory. Check your store for current availability, price, and origin.

Look for apples without bruises or decay. Natural surface markings alone don’t make a bad apple.
Refrigerate apples to help preserve their crisp texture. Check stored fruit regularly and use damaged apples promptly.
Eat fresh, slice into salads, or cook into applesauce. Fuji’s naturally sweet character suits simple preparations.
